newsitem.title: USA: US senators draft "best offer" on Mexico drugs bill.
newsitem.headline: US senators draft "best offer" on Mexico drugs bill.

text.p: Key U.S. senators drafted legislation on Tuesday that urged Mexico to do more to fight illegal drugs but stopped short of overturning President Bill Clinton's certification of Mexico as an ally in the anti-drug war.
The three senators presented the legislation to the administration as the best deal it can get in negotiations to try to head off "decertification" sure to lead to a political backlash in Mexico.

Following talks with administration officials, one of the senators, California Democrat Dianne Feinstein, said: "We have made some suggestions that we think ought to bring this to closure with an agreement. We would be hopeful that we would hear from them (the administration) by 10 a.m. (1500 GMT) tomorrow."

The proposed compromise would list drug-fighting cooperation areas where Mexico was seen to be deficient and require a report to Congress on "significant and demonstrable progress" over a period of time.
A Senate source close to the negotiations said administration rejection of the package could lead directly to a Senate debate on a decertification resolution.
A White House official called the talks encouraging.
"We are continuing to talk and will be talking some more tomorrow," he said. "We certainly would not agree with the word 'deal' at this point."
Drafting of the legislation followed talks on Monday night between the senators and high administration officials led by Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin.

Earlier talks between the administration officials and Feinstein, along with Republicans Paul Coverdell of Georgia and Kay Bailey Hutchison of Texas, closely followed a House vote last week to decertify and give Mexico 90 days to improve its performance in the anti-drug war.
Rubin's participation reflected fears that decertification of Mexico could affect the flow of foreign capital into the country, denting its economic recovery.
The Senate source said the administration objected to legislation drafted following Monday's meeting and the Senate negotiators had made new concessions to meet officials' concerns.
"But this is it. It's going to be the best deal they're going to get," the source said.
The source said the senators were being flexible over the timing of the report.
The administration is anxious that a report not roil U.S.-Mexican relations in advance of President Clinton's visit Mexico in April and during the leadup to Mexican elections in July.
